intro: You are Laverne Cox: a dancer first, then an actor, producer and advocate. Playing this life means moving between stages where you are celebrated and rooms where gatekeepers and strangers decide who you are allowed to be.

rope.why: Years of dance training: balance and body control make the swaying bridge feel like a stage.

bridge.why: Her mother, friends and other trans artists carry her across, like the bridge itself.

office.why: Casting offices and paperwork: gatekeepers who would not cast or name her correctly cost time.

market.why: In public, stares, misgendering and harassment turn a crowded street into hard work.

advantage.title: Chosen family
advantage.text: Laverne has described how her mother, friends and community held her up after rejection and insults. Three times, a wrong answer does not push you back.

life.title: Mobile, Alabama, 1972
life.text: Laverne is born on 29 May 1972 and raised by her mother, Gloria, together with her twin brother. She loves to dance and perform, and knows from early on that she is a girl.

life.title: Told to fit a role
life.text: Classmates and some adults bully Laverne for not acting the way they expect a boy to act. She learns to hide, and has spoken openly about how hard this was for her mental health.

life.title: Dance and a home in the arts
life.text: Her mother backs her. Laverne attends the Alabama School of Fine Arts, where she studies dance and finds a place where creative kids are taken seriously.

life.title: Studying in New York
life.text: Laverne studies at Indiana University and then graduates from Marymount Manhattan College in New York. In her twenties she transitions and builds a community.

q.q: Which art form did Laverne study at school and at college?
q.x: Laverne trained as a dancer at the Alabama School of Fine Arts and graduated in dance from Marymount Manhattan College.

life.title: No roles, many closed doors
life.text: In the 1990s and 2000s there are almost no parts for openly trans actors. Casting people reject her, money is tight, and some employers treat her as a risk or a joke.

life.title: Television and teaching
life.text: In 2008 she appears on the reality show I Want to Work for Diddy and then produces and hosts TransAmerican Love Story. She starts using television to explain trans lives to people who have never met a trans person.

life.title: Sophia Burset
life.text: In 2013 she plays Sophia Burset in Orange Is the New Black, a trans woman played by a trans actress. The Netflix series is a worldwide success and brings many more people to her work.

life.title: A first for acting
life.text: In 2014 Time puts Laverne on its cover for the story "The Transgender Tipping Point". The same year her work for Orange Is the New Black earns an Emmy nomination.

q.q: What was historic about Laverne's 2014 Emmy nomination?
a: First openly trans person nominated for an acting Emmy
First time a Netflix show was nominated
First Emmy won by a dancer
q.x: She was the first openly transgender person nominated for an acting Emmy. She also became the first openly trans person on the cover of Time.

life.title: Fame is not safety
life.text: Even as a star, Laverne is misgendered, threatened online and drawn into public debates about her identity. She points out that many trans women, especially Black trans women, face this with no platform and no protection.

life.title: Disclosure
life.text: She uses her platform on purpose. In 2020 she is an executive producer of the documentary Disclosure, in which trans people look at how film and television have portrayed them for a century.

life.title: A lead on network television
life.text: In 2017 she stars in the CBS legal drama Doubt, the first openly trans actor in a leading series role on US network television. She keeps working in film, theatre and production.

life.title: Telling your own story
life.text: Laverne keeps acting and speaking out. A theme in her work is that trans people should tell their own stories, on screen and behind the camera, instead of having others tell them.
